blocks.body:
Many functions are built as limits of simpler ones: $e^x$ as the limit of its Taylor polynomials, a Fourier series as the limit of finite trigonometric sums, the solution of a differential equation as the limit of successive approximations. We would like the limit to inherit the good properties of the approximations. If every $f_n$ is continuous, is the limit continuous? Is the integral of the limit equal to the limit of the integrals?

For the naive notion, pointwise convergence, both answers are no. Uniform convergence is the stronger notion under which both answers are yes, and the difference between the two comes down to the order of two quantifiers.

blocks.title: Pointwise convergence
blocks.body:
Let $E \subseteq \mathbb R$ and let $f_n, f : E \to \mathbb R$. The sequence $(f_n)$ converges pointwise to $f$ on $E$ if $f_n(x) \to f(x)$ for every $x \in E$ (see [[seq-limits]]); that is,
$$\forall x \in E\ \ \forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N\ \ \forall n \ge N: \quad |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon.$$
Here $N$ may depend on both $\varepsilon$ and $x$.

blocks.title: The standard warning: x^n
Uniform convergence
blocks.body:
The sequence $(f_n)$ converges uniformly to $f$ on $E$ if
$$\forall \varepsilon > 0\ \ \exists N\ \ \forall n \ge N\ \ \forall x \in E: \quad |f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon.$$
Writing $\|g\|_E = \sup_{x \in E}|g(x)|$, this is equivalent to $\|f_n - f\|_E \to 0$.

Now $N$ depends only on $\varepsilon$: one $N$ serves every point. Picture a band of half-width $\varepsilon$ around the graph of $f$; uniform convergence says that from some $N$ on, the entire graph of $f_n$ lies inside the band.

blocks.title: Testing for uniform convergence
blocks.body:
Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, so a sequence can only converge uniformly to its pointwise limit. In practice: first find the pointwise limit $f$, then compute or estimate $s_n = \|f_n - f\|_E$ and decide whether $s_n \to 0$.
- $f_n(x) = x^n$ on $[0, a]$ with $0 < a < 1$: $s_n = a^n \to 0$, so the convergence is uniform. On $[0, 1)$, $s_n = 1$ for every $n$, so it is not. The same sequence can converge uniformly on one set and not on a larger one.
- $f_n(x) = x/n$: on $[0, 1]$, $s_n = 1/n \to 0$, uniform. On $\mathbb R$, $|f_n|$ is unbounded, so $s_n = \infty$ and the convergence is not uniform, although $f_n(x) \to 0$ for every real $x$.
- To show that convergence is not uniform, it suffices to find points $x_n \in E$ with $|f_n(x_n) - f(x_n)|$ bounded away from $0$, as $x_n = 2^{-1/n}$ did above.

There is also a Cauchy criterion, useful because it does not require knowing the limit: $(f_n)$ converges uniformly on $E$ if and only if for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $N$ with $|f_n(x) - f_m(x)| < \varepsilon$ for all $m, n \ge N$ and all $x \in E$. If this holds, each sequence $(f_n(x))$ is Cauchy and so has a limit $f(x)$; letting $m \to \infty$ gives $|f_n(x) - f(x)| \le \varepsilon$ for all $n \ge N$ and all $x$, which is uniform convergence. The converse follows from $|f_n - f_m| \le |f_n - f| + |f - f_m|$.

blocks.title: Uniform limits of continuous functions are continuous
blocks.body: Let $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $E$. If every $f_n$ is continuous at a point $c \in E$, then $f$ is continuous at $c$. In particular, a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.

Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Choose one $n$ with $|f_n(x) - f(x)| < \varepsilon/3$ for all $x \in E$; this is where uniformity is used. Since $f_n$ is continuous at $c$ ([[continuity]]), there is $\delta > 0$ with $|f_n(x) - f_n(c)| < \varepsilon/3$ whenever $x \in E$ and $|x - c| < \delta$. For such $x$,
$$|f(x) - f(c)| \le |f(x) - f_n(x)| + |f_n(x) - f_n(c)| + |f_n(c) - f(c)| < \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} + \tfrac{\varepsilon}{3} = \varepsilon.$$
With only pointwise convergence, the $n$ that makes the first term small would depend on $x$, and then so would $\delta$; and $x^n$ on $[0, 1]$ shows that the conclusion really can fail. Read backwards, the theorem gives a second proof that $x^n$ does not converge uniformly on $[0,1]$: its limit is discontinuous.

blocks.title: Integrals of uniform limits
blocks.body:
Let each $f_n$ be continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $[a, b]$. Then $f$ is continuous and
$$\lim_{n \to \infty} \int_a^b f_n(x)\,dx = \int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

By the previous theorem $f$ is continuous, so it is integrable ([[riemann-integral]]). For every $n$,
$$\left| \int_a^b f_n - \int_a^b f \right| \le \int_a^b |f_n - f| \le (b - a)\,\|f_n - f\|_{[a,b]},$$
and the right-hand side tends to $0$.

blocks.title: Weierstrass M-test
blocks.body: Let $f_k : E \to \mathbb R$, and suppose there are constants $M_k$ with $|f_k(x)| \le M_k$ for all $x \in E$ and $\sum_{k=1}^\infty M_k < \infty$. Then $\sum_{k=1}^\infty f_k(x)$ converges absolutely for every $x \in E$, and the partial sums $S_n = \sum_{k=1}^n f_k$ converge uniformly on $E$.

For each $x$ the series converges absolutely by comparison with $\sum M_k$ ([[series]]); call its sum $S(x)$. For every $x \in E$ and every $n$,
$$|S(x) - S_n(x)| = \Big|\sum_{k > n} f_k(x)\Big| \le \sum_{k > n} |f_k(x)| \le \sum_{k > n} M_k.$$
The right-hand side does not depend on $x$, and it tends to $0$ as $n \to \infty$ because it is the tail of a convergent series. Hence $\|S - S_n\|_E \to 0$.

Combined with the first theorem: if each $f_k$ is continuous, so is the sum. For example $\sum_{k \ge 1} \sin(kx)/k^2$ is continuous on $\mathbb R$, with $M_k = 1/k^2$.

blocks.title: Derivatives need more
blocks.body:
Uniform convergence of $f_n$ says nothing about $f_n'$. Let $f_n(x) = \sin(nx)/\sqrt n$. Then $\|f_n\|_{\mathbb R} = 1/\sqrt n \to 0$, so $f_n \to 0$ uniformly on $\mathbb R$, yet $f_n'(x) = \sqrt n \cos(nx)$, which equals $\sqrt n \to \infty$ at $x = 0$. Small wiggles can have steep slopes.

The correct statement puts the hypothesis on the derivatives. Suppose each $f_n$ is continuously differentiable on $[a, b]$, the derivatives $f_n'$ converge uniformly on $[a, b]$ to a function $g$, and $f_n(x_0)$ converges for one point $x_0 \in [a, b]$. Then $f_n$ converges uniformly on $[a,b]$ to a differentiable function $f$ with $f' = g$.

Proof: $g$ is continuous, as a uniform limit of continuous functions. Let $c = \lim f_n(x_0)$ and define $f(x) = c + \int_{x_0}^x g(t)\,dt$; by the [[ftc|fundamental theorem of calculus]], $f' = g$. Also $f_n(x) = f_n(x_0) + \int_{x_0}^x f_n'(t)\,dt$, so for all $x \in [a, b]$,
$$|f_n(x) - f(x)| \le |f_n(x_0) - c| + (b - a)\,\|f_n' - g\|_{[a,b]},$$
and the right-hand side tends to $0$ independently of $x$. (The result remains true without assuming the $f_n'$ continuous, with a proof based on the [[mvt|mean value theorem]]; see Rudin, Chapter 7.)

blocks.title: A sliding bump
blocks.body: Let $f_n(x) = \dfrac{nx}{1 + n^2x^2}$. Show that $f_n \to 0$ pointwise on $[0, 1]$ but not uniformly, and that the convergence is uniform on $[\delta, 1]$ for every $0 < \delta < 1$.
blocks.solution:
Pointwise: $f_n(0) = 0$, and for $x > 0$,
$$0 \le f_n(x) \le \frac{nx}{n^2x^2} = \frac{1}{nx} \to 0.$$
Not uniform: at $x_n = 1/n$ we get $f_n(1/n) = \frac{1}{1 + 1} = \frac12$ for every $n$, so $\|f_n\|_{[0,1]} \ge \frac12$. In fact $\frac12$ is the maximum, since $1 + n^2x^2 \ge 2nx$ by AM–GM. Each $f_n$ is a bump of height $\frac12$ located at $x = 1/n$: the bump slides into the endpoint $0$ but never shrinks.

Uniform on $[\delta, 1]$: the same bound gives $0 \le f_n(x) \le \dfrac{1}{nx} \le \dfrac{1}{n\delta}$ for all $x \in [\delta, 1]$, and $\dfrac{1}{n\delta} \to 0$ independently of $x$.

Note that the limit function $0$ is continuous, yet the convergence on $[0, 1]$ is not uniform. A continuous limit does not imply uniform convergence.

blocks.title: A limit and an integral that do not commute
blocks.body: Let $f_n(x) = nx(1 - x^2)^n$ on $[0, 1]$. Find $\lim_{n\to\infty} f_n(x)$ for each $x$, and $\lim_{n\to\infty} \int_0^1 f_n(x)\,dx$.
blocks.solution:
At $x = 0$ and $x = 1$, $f_n(x) = 0$. For $0 < x < 1$ put $q = 1 - x^2 \in (0, 1)$; then $f_n(x) = x \cdot nq^n \to 0$, because $nq^n \to 0$ for $0 < q < 1$ (the ratio of consecutive terms, $\frac{n+1}{n}q$, tends to $q < 1$). So $f_n \to 0$ pointwise, and the integral of the limit is $0$.

For the integrals substitute $u = 1 - x^2$, $du = -2x\,dx$:
$$\int_0^1 nx(1 - x^2)^n\,dx = \frac n2\int_0^1 u^n\,du = \frac{n}{2(n + 1)} \to \frac12.$$
So $\lim \int_0^1 f_n = \frac12 \ne 0 = \int_0^1 \lim f_n$. By the integral theorem the convergence cannot be uniform. Directly: at $x_n = 1/\sqrt n$,
$$f_n(x_n) = \sqrt n\Big(1 - \frac1n\Big)^n \ge \frac{\sqrt n}{4} \quad (n \ge 2),$$
because $(1 - \frac1n)^n$ increases with $n$ and equals $\frac14$ at $n = 2$. The functions develop ever taller spikes near $0$ that carry a fixed amount of area.

blocks.title: Summing a series by integrating term by term
blocks.solution:
Start from the geometric series $\sum_{j=0}^\infty t^j = \dfrac{1}{1 - t}$ for $|t| < 1$. On $[0, \frac12]$ we have $|t^j| \le 2^{-j}$ and $\sum_j 2^{-j} = 2 < \infty$, so by the M-test the partial sums $S_n(t) = \sum_{j=0}^n t^j$ converge uniformly to $\frac{1}{1-t}$ on $[0, \frac12]$. Each $S_n$ is continuous, so the integral theorem gives
$$\int_0^{1/2}\frac{dt}{1 - t} = \lim_{n\to\infty}\int_0^{1/2}\sum_{j=0}^n t^j\,dt = \lim_{n\to\infty}\sum_{j=0}^n \frac{(1/2)^{j+1}}{j + 1} = \sum_{k=1}^\infty \frac{1}{k\,2^k}.$$
The left-hand side is $\big[-\ln(1 - t)\big]_0^{1/2} = -\ln\frac12 = \ln 2$.

The same argument with $-t$ in place of $t$, on $[0, x]$ for $0 \le x < 1$, gives $\ln(1 + x) = x - \frac{x^2}{2} + \frac{x^3}{3} - \cdots$. At $x = 1$ the M-test is no longer available, and in fact $\sum (-t)^j$ does not converge uniformly on $[0, 1)$: the error of its $n$-th partial sum is $\frac{t^{n+1}}{1+t}$ in absolute value, and its supremum over $[0, 1)$ is $\frac12$ for every $n$. But uniform convergence is a sufficient condition, not a necessary one. Here the error can be integrated directly:
$$\Big|\ln 2 - \sum_{k=1}^{n+1}\frac{(-1)^{k+1}}{k}\Big| = \int_0^1 \frac{t^{n+1}}{1+t}\,dt \le \int_0^1 t^{n+1}\,dt = \frac{1}{n+2} \to 0,$$
so $1 - \frac12 + \frac13 - \cdots = \ln 2$. A general tool for such endpoint questions is Abel's theorem, stated in [[power-series]].

blocks.body:
- Uniform convergence depends on the set. $x^n \to 0$ uniformly on $[0, 0.9]$ but not on $[0, 1)$; $x/n \to 0$ uniformly on $[0, 1]$ but not on $\mathbb R$. Always say where.
- A continuous limit does not imply uniform convergence: the sliding bump $nx/(1 + n^2x^2)$ tends to the continuous function $0$, not uniformly on $[0,1]$. There is a partial converse, Dini's theorem: if continuous functions on a compact set increase (or decrease) pointwise to a continuous limit, the convergence is uniform ([[compactness]]).
- On an unbounded interval, uniform convergence does not justify swapping limit and integral. $f_n(x) = \frac1n e^{-x/n}$ tends to $0$ uniformly on $[0, \infty)$ (its supremum is $\frac1n$), yet $\int_0^\infty f_n = 1$ for every $n$. The bound $(b - a)\|f_n - f\|$ is useless when $b - a = \infty$; see [[improper-integrals]].
- Uniform convergence of $f_n$ does not give convergence of $f_n'$; it is the derivatives that must converge uniformly.

A power series $\sum a_kx^k$ with radius of convergence $R$ converges uniformly on $[-r, r]$ for every $0 < r < R$, by the M-test, which is why it can be integrated and differentiated term by term ([[power-series]], [[taylor]]). For Fourier series the question of when and in what sense the series converges is much subtler ([[fourier-poisson]]). The continuous functions on $[a, b]$ with the distance $\|f - g\|_{[a,b]}$ form a complete [[metric-spaces|metric space]], because a uniformly Cauchy sequence has a uniform limit and that limit is continuous; the Weierstrass approximation theorem says the polynomials are dense in it.

When uniform convergence fails, the [[lebesgue|Lebesgue integral]] supplies the monotone and dominated convergence theorems, which justify swapping limit and integral under far weaker hypotheses. In complex analysis, limits of [[holomorphic]] functions that are uniform on compact sets are again holomorphic, which is used to show that series such as $\sum n^{-s}$ define analytic functions ([[zeta]]).

1. Does $f_n(x) = \dfrac{x}{1 + nx^2}$ converge uniformly on $\mathbb R$? (Find the maximum of $|f_n|$.)
2. Show that $f_n(x) = x^n(1 - x)$ converges uniformly to $0$ on $[0, 1]$.
3. Prove that $\sum_{k=1}^\infty \dfrac{\cos(kx)}{k^3}$ defines a continuous function on $\mathbb R$ that may be integrated term by term over $[0, \pi]$.
4. Give an example of discontinuous functions $f_n$ that converge uniformly on $\mathbb R$ to a continuous function.
